fixes.explanation: You've got it, baker. Saul was Israel's king before David (1 Samuel 11:15; 2 Samuel 5:3), and David says, “…for we did not inquire of Him in the days of Saul.” David also asks the leaders if this is of the LORD their God (verse 2). I respect a man who checks first, because I've skipped the recipe before and learned that lesson with flour on my hat.

That's a juicy story, but it's not in this passage. The text never says Saul hid anything. David's reason is that “…we did not inquire of Him in the days of Saul.” Saul was Israel's king before David (1 Samuel 11:15; 2 Samuel 5:3). David's reason is about them, not a secret.

This passage never mentions a promise from Saul. Saul was Israel's king before David (1 Samuel 11:15; 2 Samuel 5:3). What David says is, “…for we did not inquire of Him in the days of Saul.” That's the whole reason he gives. I'd say it's a pretty honest one.

True! The text says, “And because this proposal seemed right to all the people, the whole assembly agreed to it.” A whole assembly on the same page is a beautiful thing. Even my cookie cutter kids couldn't agree on a topping.

Not false, friend. The text says, “And because this proposal seemed right to all the people, the whole assembly agreed to it.” The proposal seemed right to all the people. So the whole assembly said yes.

A new cart is right! Verse 7 says, “So they carried the ark of God from the house of Abinadab on a new cart…” Abinadab's house is where they pick the ark up. I know a thing or two about being replaced by something shinier, since a new stamper took my spot on the Millers' counter, so I notice a new cart.

That sounds fancy, but the text doesn't say it. They carried the ark “…from the house of Abinadab on a new cart…” That's a cart, not a chariot. David is the king (2 Samuel 5:3), and he's right there in the crowd celebrating.
The text names a different ride. It says they carried the ark from the house of Abinadab “…on a new cart, with Uzzah and Ahio guiding the cart.” Camels aren't mentioned. The oxen come up in verse 9.

Yes, and this is where the story turns. The text says, “…Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark, because the oxen had stumbled.” Uzzah is one of the two men guiding the cart. One moment David and all the Israelites are celebrating, and then Uzzah reaches out. I think this is the part where everybody holds their breath.

No shouting is mentioned. The text says, “…Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark, because the oxen had stumbled.” Uzzah is one of the two men guiding the cart. What the text says he does is reach out with his hand.

Joyful isn't the word the text uses here. It says, “Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah.” The songs and the harps come earlier, in verse 8. I think this one is heavy, and it's okay to say so.

The text gives a different word for David. It says, “Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah.” Anger is what the passage names. I think this is a heavy part of the story.

That's his question. The text says that day David feared God and asked, “How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?” The big plan he started with now has a big question on it. I think David is thinking hard about what just happened.

That's a sensible question, but David doesn't ask it. The text says that day David feared God and asked, “How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?” His question is about bringing the ark to him, not about who guides the cart.

The passage never says anything about a burial. What it says is that David feared God and asked, “How can I ever bring the ark of God to me?” That's the only question David asks here. It's about the ark.

Not this time, baker. The text says, “So he did not move the ark with him to the City of David; instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.” The City of David was the plan, but David did not move the ark there. He took it aside to Obed-edom's house instead.

That's the one! The text says, “Thus the ark of God remained with the family of Obed-edom in his house for three months, and the LORD blessed his household and everything he owned.” The blessing comes during those three months with the ark. I think a blessing like that is a sweet thing to read after such a heavy moment.

That's not what happens in this passage. The text says the ark remained with the family of Obed-edom for three months, “…and the LORD blessed his household and everything he owned.” So what it says about his household is a blessing, not sickness. I think that's a relief after the last few verses. The story isn't over yet.
